title: Stasimon 4 (lines 884–923)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus compares Antigone to figures of myth who suffered by fate, imprisoned or blinded: Danae, shut away; Dryas' child, the Edonian king (Lycurgus), brought by Bacchus to a rocky dungeon (lines 897–900); and two step-sons blinded by a jealous step-mother (lines 910–913). No one escapes Fate.

Like to thee that maiden bright,
Danaë, in her brass-bound tower,
Once exchanged the glad sunlight
For a cell, her bridal bower.
And yet she sprang of royal line,
My child, like thine,

anchorPassages.note: Further imprisoned sufferers. Trimmed to end before pending text fix at line 917.
anchorPassages.text:
Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King,
For words of high disdain
Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring,
To cool the madness of a fevered brain.
His frenzy passed,
He learnt at last
’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire;
And of the tuneful Nine provoked the ire.
By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main,
On Bosporus’ lone strand,
Where stretcheth Salmydessus’ plain
In the wild Thracian land,
There on his borders Ares witnessèd
The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en
The gore that trickled from a spindle red,
The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.
Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom,
The blasted issue of their mother’s womb.

analysis.weDoWords: “Rash”, “high disdain” and “rocky dungeon” stand out in lines 897–900. ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom, / The blasted issue of their mother’s womb.

segments.script: Today we saw how allusion shapes others who were shut away. Key takeaway: The myths show gods imprisoning mortals who showed “high disdain,” so divine punishment of human pride hangs over Creon as much as over Antigone.

objective: Students will summarize what happens in Stasimon 4 (lines 884–923) (others who were shut away) in 2 sentences and, in a 3-sentence warm-up response, explain how one quoted line from the scene sets up the scene that follows.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: Retell the most important events of “Stasimon 4 (lines 884–923)” in order, one sentence for each event.
items.lookFor: The Chorus compares Antigone to figures of myth who suffered by fate, imprisoned or blinded: Danae, shut away; Dryas' child, the Edonian king (Lycurgus), brought by Bacchus to a rocky dungeon (lines 897–900); and two step-sons blinded by a jealous step-mother (lines 910–913). No one escapes Fate.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The Chorus compares Antigone to figures of myth who suffered by fate, imprisoned or blinded: Danae, shut away; Dryas' child, the Edonian king (Lycurgus), brought by Bacchus to a rocky dungeon (lines 897–900); and two step-sons blinded by a jealous step-mother (lines 910–913). No one escapes Fate.

items.text: Why include a king (Lycurgus) among the examples?
items.lookFor: A king as well as a young woman can be shut away; cite the Lycurgus stanza.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Among the examples is “Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King,” whom Bacchus shut in a “rocky dungeon” for “words of high disdain” (lines 897–900). By including a king who insulted a god, the ode hints that rulers, not only young women, can be locked away by fate—an implicit warning beside Creon.

items.text: What does “Stasimon 4 (lines 884–923)” suggest about others who were shut away? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: Myth makes Antigone part of a long pattern of suffering and implies that even the powerful cannot escape fate, a warning to Creon.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Myth makes Antigone part of a long pattern of suffering and implies that even the powerful cannot escape fate, a warning to Creon. Evidence to accept: “Strange are the ways of Fate, her power / Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; / Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea / From Fate can flee” (Stasimon 4, lines 893–896): Chorus, lines 893–896. Credit any reading that quotes the text and explains it.
